transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, what brings me in is that I’ve gotten stuck doing these little routines lately. Like, I find myself having to wash my hands again every time after handling my wrist brace. I had to get this brace, you see, because I was doing some heavy pruning out in the garden. We have these massive hydrangeas—my wife and I planted them back in '98. Beautiful blue ones, though you know, the soil acidity changed a few years back and they turned pink, which is actually pretty fascinating chemically, but... where was I? 

Oh, right, the routines. So I wash my hands, and then I find myself rechecking the stove, and the front door. And I do this silent counting through all my steps before I can actually leave the house. I used to teach history, you see, so I’m very used to keeping track of details and timelines. I remember this one semester I had 300 students in a lecture hall and I had to count the exams by hand... I suppose I've always been a bit meticulous. 

But anyway, doing all this checking and counting now, it’s starting to make me late for things. I'll be standing there, and even when I know perfectly well I’ve already done enough and everything is fine, I just have to do it all over again.
Do you feel anxious or upset when you're unable to complete these routines?

Anxious? Well, I'm not entirely sure. I suppose I haven't really been in a situation where I *couldn't* complete them, because I just... make sure I do them. Even if it makes me late. 

Though, if someone interrupts me—like when the phone rings right when I'm in the middle of checking the stove—I suppose I get a bit flustered. It's usually those telemarketers, you know. They always seem to call right at the absolute worst times. I read a fascinating piece in the paper recently about how those automated dialing systems work. It's all algorithms now, dialing thousands of numbers a minute. It reminds me of the Industrial Revolution, really, the relentless automation of human labor. I used to teach a whole seminar on the mechanization of the textile industry in 19th-century Britain. The Luddites actually had a very valid point about the disruption of daily life, it wasn't just about smashing machines... 

But, I'm sorry, I've lost the thread. What did you ask me? Something about getting upset?
Do you feel like doing these routines helps you feel better or prevents something bad from happening?

Does it prevent something bad? Well, like I was saying earlier about getting stuck in those little routines—the hand washing with the brace, checking the stove and the front door, the silent counting—I know perfectly well I've already done enough, but I just have to do them anyway. I don't know if it makes me feel *better*, exactly, but I just have to finish the sequence. Even when it makes me late. 

Being late used to be my absolute biggest pet peeve, you know. Back when I was teaching, I had a very strict policy about tardiness. If you weren't in your seat when the lecture started, that was it. I always made sure I was early, too. I used to commute to the campus in this old 1984 Volvo 240. Built like an absolute tank, that car. Swedish engineering was really unparalleled back then. Did you know Volvo actually invented the three-point seatbelt and just gave the patent away for free? They essentially open-sourced it to save lives. You simply don't see that kind of corporate ethics anymore. Today it's all planned obsolescence, everything is designed to break in a few years so you're forced into buying a replacement. It's a terrible waste of natural resources, really, the amount of electronic waste we produce...

But... oh dear, I'm rambling again, aren't I? I always do that. What did you just ask me? Something about why I do the counting?
Do you think something specific would happen if you didn't complete these routines?

Would something specific happen? Well... it's not so much that I think the house will explode or anything dramatic like that. It's more... I'll be sitting at home reading, or getting ready to head down for my volunteer shift at the history museum—I do the docent tours on Thursdays, mostly the local industrial history exhibit. We just got this fascinating new donation of late 19th-century milling equipment. The craftsmanship on those old gears is just extraordinary. They used cast iron back then, you know, poured right into sand molds. The foundry process was incredibly dangerous work, the heat and the fumes... quite a few workers ended up with respiratory issues, which actually led to some of the very first labor safety movements in this state... 

But, right, the routines. I'll just be sitting there, getting ready to go, and this... this ugly little thought just keeps barging into my head. It just insists that I've left something unsafe, or that I've touched something unclean, or that I've somehow put someone at risk by not checking. I know perfectly well it's completely out of proportion, but the thought just won't leave me alone until I go back and do the counting and the checking. 

It's terribly distracting, really. Especially when I'm trying to read. I've been trying to get through this new biography of Ulysses S. Grant. Did you know he actually wrote his memoirs while he was dying of throat cancer? Mark Twain helped him publish them so his family wouldn't be left destitute. It's an incredible story of perseverance... but I can barely get through a chapter lately without that nagging feeling that I need to go check the stove again.
Do these ugly little thoughts appear before you start your counting and checking routines?

Yes, precisely. Like I was just saying a moment ago, they always happen first. I'll be sitting there trying to read, or getting my coat on for the museum, and that thought just barges in before I do anything else. It just insists I've touched something unclean or left a burner on, and that I've somehow put someone at risk. I know it's completely out of proportion, but it triggers the whole routine. 

Though, speaking of unclean... the dust on some of those older books can be quite something. I have a rather extensive collection of historical volumes in my study, and they require quite a bit of upkeep. The binding on the late 19th-century ones is just exquisite, though. They used genuine Moroccan leather, you know, and the gold leaf stamping... bookbinding is such a lost art. Now everything is just mass-produced with cheap glue that cracks after a few years. It's a terrible shame how we've devalued physical media. I was actually discussing this with the head archivist at the museum just last week—how digital records are actually far more fragile than paper in the long run. If the servers go down or the file formats become obsolete, you lose everything. Whereas a good vellum manuscript can last a millennium...

But, oh dear. I've completely lost track again, haven't I? I'm so sorry. What did you ask me? Something about when the thoughts start?
Would you describe these ugly little thoughts as unwelcome or uninvited when they appear?

Unwelcome? Oh, absolutely. Completely uninvited. Like I said, I'll just be sitting quietly in my armchair reading, or putting my coat on to head down to the museum for my shift, and it just... barges right in. This ugly little thought that I've left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, or that I'm putting someone at risk. I know perfectly well it's completely out of proportion, but it just intrudes on whatever I'm doing. 

It's remarkably similar to how people used to just drop by unannounced back in the day, isn't it? When I was growing up in the fifties, neighbors would just walk right up to the screen door and let themselves in. My mother always had a pot of coffee on the stove just in case. Percolator coffee, of course. None of these pod machines you see everywhere now. Have you seen the statistics on how much plastic waste those single-use coffee pods generate? It's staggering. Millions of them ending up in landfills every single day, and they take something like five hundred years to decompose. We're leaving an absolute ecological disaster for our grandchildren, all for the sake of saving two minutes in the morning. I actually read a fascinating article in National Geographic about microplastics being found in the Mariana Trench...

But... forgive me. I've done it again. You were asking about the thoughts being uninvited, weren't you? Yes, they are entirely unwelcome.
Do you feel like these ugly little thoughts are a part of yourself or do they feel alien to you?

Are they a part of me, or alien? Hmm. I'm not entirely sure how to answer that, to be honest. I've never really stopped to categorize them like that. They're just... there in my head, so I suppose they're coming from me, but I don't really know. 

It's funny you use the word alien, though. We actually just hosted a guest lecturer at the museum last month who spoke extensively about the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798. John Adams signed them into law during the Quasi-War with France. The political paranoia of the time was just extraordinary. The newspapers were incredibly partisan—makes today's media look quite tame by comparison, actually. They used these massive printing presses back then, where every single letter had to be typeset by hand. Can you imagine the patience that required? The apprentices, usually just young boys, would have their hands permanently stained with ink. It was a mixture of lampblack and linseed oil, mostly. 

Linseed oil has such a distinct smell, doesn't it? My grandfather used to use it to treat the wood on his old fishing boat up in Maine. We used to go out on the water every summer when I was a boy. He had this beautiful wooden skiff that he built himself. The craftsmanship of hand-built wooden boats is something you just don't see anymore. Now everything is fiberglass and molded plastic. It lacks a certain... soul, I think. 

But... oh, my apologies. I've sailed right off course again, haven't I? You were asking... oh dear, what were you asking? Something about whether I felt like an alien?
How much distress do these ugly little thoughts cause you when they appear?

Distress? Well, yes, it is distressing. Like I keep saying, I'll just be sitting there reading at home, or getting ready for my museum shift, and that ugly little thought just keeps barging in—telling me I've left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, and that I've somehow put someone at risk. Even though I know perfectly well it's completely out of proportion, it creates this... this lingering unease that I just can't shake. It's a very nagging sort of anxiety. 

It’s a very particular sort of dread, really. Actually, it reminds me a bit of the general atmosphere of unease we had when I was a boy in the early sixties. I remember the air raid drills at school so vividly. We'd have to hide under our wooden desks, which is rather comical in hindsight—as if a half-inch of oak was going to protect us from a nuclear blast! My father actually built a small fallout shelter in our basement. He stocked it with hundreds of those heavy tin cans of survival crackers and water. 

The history of canning is absolutely fascinating, by the way. It was pioneered by a man named Nicolas Appert during the Napoleonic Wars, because the French army desperately needed a way to preserve food for their long campaigns. They used glass jars sealed with wax at first, long before tin cans were even invented. Of course, when they did move to tin cans later in the 19th century, they sealed them with lead solder, which led to some truly disastrous consequences for early explorers. The Franklin Expedition, for instance—they got stuck in the Arctic ice in 1845, and it's widely believed that many of the men went mad from lead poisoning leaching from their tinned provisions. Imagine being stranded in the ice, thousands of miles from home, slowly losing your mind to your own food supply...

Oh, good heavens. I'm rambling about the Arctic now, aren't I? I do apologize, my mind just completely wandered off the map. What were we talking about? You asked how much something bothers me, I think?
Do you feel like these thoughts are in line with your own beliefs and values, or do they seem to contradict them?

Values? Oh, no, they certainly don't feel like they align with my values at all. I mean, I'm a very careful, conscientious person. I care deeply about not causing harm or making a mess of things, which is why it's so bothersome when these thoughts just pop in and insist I've done exactly that. They contradict how I try to live my life entirely.

It’s a bit like... well, it’s like the preservation standards we use at the museum. We have incredibly strict protocols for handling the artifacts. You always wear the white cotton gloves, you monitor the humidity levels constantly—usually keeping it around fifty percent relative humidity, depending on the material, of course. Paper degrades terribly if it's too damp. We have a collection of letters from the Civil War era, written by a local regiment, and the paper is so brittle now. It's mostly rag paper, which actually holds up better than the wood pulp paper they started using later in the nineteenth century. 

Wood pulp paper is full of lignin, you see, which is what makes old paperbacks turn yellow and crumble. It actually produces acid as it breaks down, essentially destroying itself from the inside out. They have to use mass deacidification processes now to save millions of books in libraries around the world. They literally pump an alkaline vapor into these giant vacuum chambers full of books to neutralize the acid. It’s a fascinating intersection of chemistry and history, really. I read a whole book on the history of paper making once. Did you know the Chinese were making paper out of mulberry bark thousands of years before it caught on in Europe? They kept it a closely guarded secret for centuries...

Oh, dear. I've done it again. The Silk Road, paper making... I am so sorry, doctor. My mind is just a runaway train today. You were asking about my values, I believe? Yes, they contradict them entirely.
Do you feel like doing these routines helps to prevent or reduce the anxiety caused by these ugly little thoughts?

Help? Well, yes, I suppose that's exactly why I do them. That's actually what brings me in today, to be quite honest. I’ve gotten so stuck doing these little routines just to quiet that anxiety down. I'll find myself washing my hands all over again after I've handled my wrist brace, or I'll have to go back and recheck the stove and the front door. Sometimes I even have to silently count through my steps before I can finally leave the house. It temporarily stops the dread, but it's starting to make me late for things, even when I know perfectly well I’ve already done enough. 

It’s terribly frustrating, being late. I've always prided myself on punctuality. In fact, we have a rather magnificent collection of antique timepieces at the museum. Pocket watches, mostly, from the 18th and 19th centuries. There's one particular piece, a French carriage clock from around 1840, that is just a marvel of engineering. The escapement mechanism is so delicate, so precise. 

Clockmaking was such a highly respected profession back then. Before the railroads standardized time zones in the 1880s, every town basically kept its own local time based on high noon. Can you imagine the chaos of trying to schedule a train when New York time was twelve minutes ahead of Philadelphia time? The railroad companies finally had to step in and divide the country into four time zones just to keep the trains from colliding. It was a massive logistical undertaking, completely changing how humanity perceived time. Before that, people just lived by the sun. It's a much more natural rhythm, don't you think? Waking with the dawn, sleeping when it gets dark... 

Oh, for heaven's sake. I'm off on another excursion, aren't I? Time zones and carriage clocks... I am so sorry. You were asking if the routines help the anxiety? Yes, they do help in the moment, but then I end up running late because I can't stop doing them.
Do you feel like these ugly little thoughts are something that you would normally think, or are they completely foreign to your usual way of thinking?

Foreign? Oh, completely foreign. They aren't my thoughts at all, not really. I mean, I would never normally think such things. It's like they've been dropped into my head by an outside force. I'm a very rational person, generally speaking. I like order and logic, which is probably why I enjoy cataloging things so much. 

Actually, speaking of cataloging, I spent hours yesterday trying to organize my collection of vintage postcards. I have hundreds of them, mostly from the early 1900s. There's this one specific set from the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis that I'm particularly fond of. The architecture of those temporary pavilions was just astounding. They built these massive, ornate structures out of a mixture of plaster and hemp called staff, knowing full well they would only last a few months. It was all designed to be ephemeral. 

The Ferris wheel they had there was actually the original one from the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, dismantled and moved by train. George Washington Gale Ferris Jr. designed it to rival the Eiffel Tower, you know. It could hold over two thousand people at once! Each car was the size of a streetcar. It's a tragedy they eventually demolished it and sold it for scrap metal. Just imagine the historical value it would have today if they had managed to preserve it. We are so quick to discard our history, don't you think? We just tear things down to build something new, without a second thought for the craftsmanship of the past...

Oh, dear me. I've completely lost the thread again, haven't I? The Ferris wheel... I am so sorry, doctor. I don't know why I keep doing this. You asked if the thoughts were foreign to me? Yes, absolutely. Completely out of character for me.
Do you feel like these ugly little thoughts are something that you would normally think, or are they completely at odds with your own self-image?

At odds? Oh, entirely. I think we just touched on that, actually, but yes—they are completely at odds with how I see myself. I've always viewed myself as a careful, rational man. I certainly don't see myself as someone who would just carelessly leave a stove on to burn down a building, or fail to wash my hands and spread some awful disease. It’s completely contradictory to my nature.

My nature has always been very precise, you see. Even when I was a boy, I used to organize my father's tool bench for him. He was a carpenter, and he had these beautiful, heavy wooden planes. Hand planes, you know, for smoothing wood. Some of them were Stanley Baileys from the early 1900s. The steel in those old blades was just exceptional. You could hone them to an edge so sharp you could shave with it. 

People don't appreciate good steel anymore. Now everything is just stamped out in a factory, meant to be thrown away when it gets dull. But a good hand plane, if you take care of it, if you keep the sole perfectly flat and the iron sharp, it will last generations. You have to understand the grain of the wood, too. If you plane against the grain, you'll get tear-out, and it ruins the surface. It requires patience and a real understanding of the material. Wood is a living thing, even after it's been cut. It expands and contracts with the seasons...

Oh, good heavens. Woodworking now. I really must apologize, doctor. I seem to be completely incapable of staying on track today. You were asking about my self-image? Yes, those thoughts are entirely at odds with who I am. I am so sorry for rambling again.
Can you ever stop yourself from thinking these ugly little thoughts once they start?

Stop them? No, I really can't. That's the most maddening part of it all. I’ll just be sitting quietly at home, perhaps reading, or getting ready for my shift at the museum, and one of those ugly little thoughts just barges right in. It insists that I’ve left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, or somehow put someone at risk. And it just plays on a loop, even though I know perfectly well it’s entirely out of proportion to reality. 

It reminds me a bit of the player pianos we have in the museum's mechanical music exhibit. Have you ever seen one up close? They use these perforated paper rolls to dictate the notes. The pneumatic mechanisms read the holes in the paper and trigger the keys automatically. Once you start pumping the pedals, the music just plays, whether you want it to or not, until the roll is finished. 

The history of those paper rolls is fascinating, actually. They paved the way for early computer programming. Joseph Marie Jacquard used a similar punch-card system for his textile looms in the early 1800s. He figured out how to automate complex weaving patterns. The silk weavers in Lyon were absolutely furious, of course. They thought the machines were going to put them all out of work. They used to throw their wooden shoes—their sabots—into the machinery to break it. That's actually where the word "sabotage" comes from. Isn't that remarkable? How a piece of footwear became synonymous with deliberate destruction...

Oh, dear. I've done it again, haven't I? Sabotage and player pianos. I do apologize, doctor. You asked if I could stop the thoughts once they start. No, I can't. They just keep barging in, completely uninvited.
Do you feel like these thoughts are something that you would normally think about, or are they completely inconsistent with your own beliefs and values?

Inconsistent? Yes, entirely. I believe we were just talking about my nature, but yes, these thoughts are completely against my values. I value safety, care, and responsibility. I would never intentionally harm anyone or leave things in a dangerous state. It's completely contrary to everything I believe in. 

I've always held a deep respect for preservation, you see. That's why I worked at the museum for so many years before I retired. Preserving history is a sacred duty. We have this one exhibit, a collection of Victorian mourning jewelry, that requires the utmost care. Have you ever seen any? They used to weave the hair of the deceased into these intricate little brooches and watch fobs. It sounds macabre to modern sensibilities, but it was a deeply sentimental practice back then. 

They would boil the hair with soda and water to clean it, and then weave it over little wire molds. Sometimes they would incorporate seed pearls, which symbolized tears, or black enamel. Queen Victoria really popularized the trend after Prince Albert died. She wore black for the rest of her life, you know. Forty years of mourning. The entire country followed suit. The etiquette surrounding mourning was incredibly rigid. There were specific fabrics you had to wear—crape, mostly, because it didn't reflect light. You couldn't even use shiny black buttons for the first year and a day...

Oh, good grief. Mourning jewelry now. I am so terribly sorry, doctor. My mind just wanders off on these little excursions, and I completely lose my place. You were asking if the thoughts were inconsistent with my beliefs? Yes, absolutely. They go against everything I stand for. I do apologize for drifting off again.
Can you ever stop yourself from thinking about these things once they start, or do they continue against your will?

Stop them? No, I... I really thought we just went over this, doctor. But no, I can't stop them once they start. They just keep going, completely against my will. It's like a runaway train. 

Speaking of trains, did you know that the early steam locomotives didn't have brakes on the wheels themselves? They had to rely on the engine's tender to slow them down, or just reverse the steam pressure. It was incredibly dangerous. There was this one famous incident, the Montparnasse derailment in Paris, back in 1895. The train came into the station too fast, crashed right through the buffers, crossed the concourse, and smashed through the glass wall of the station. The engine actually fell down onto the street below. 

They took the most remarkable photographs of it. It looks almost surreal, this massive steam engine just resting on its nose in the middle of a Parisian street. The driver had been trying to make up for lost time, you see. He was running late, and he just came in too hot. The Westinghouse air brake had been invented by then—George Westinghouse patented it in 1869, I believe—but it wasn't universally adopted yet in Europe. The air brake was a marvel, really. It used compressed air to apply brakes to all the cars simultaneously, which made long freight trains possible. Before that, they had brakemen who had to run along the roofs of the moving cars, turning hand wheels to set the brakes on each individual car. Can you imagine? Running on top of a moving train in the dead of winter...

Oh, for heaven's sake. Steam trains now. I am so sorry, doctor. I've completely lost the thread again. You were asking if the thoughts continue against my will? Yes, they absolutely do. I can't stop them at all. I apologize for repeating myself, and for the tangent. My mind is just... well, it's just running away with me today.
Do you feel like these ugly little thoughts are a part of you or something separate from yourself?

Separate from myself? Well, yes and no, I suppose. I mean, they are in my head, obviously, so they must be a part of me on some level. But they don't *feel* like me. They feel like... intruders. Like something alien that's just set up camp in my mind. 

It reminds me of the cuckoo bird, actually. Have you ever read about their nesting habits? It's called brood parasitism. The female cuckoo doesn't build her own nest. Instead, she finds the nest of a different species—a reed warbler, perhaps, or a meadow pipit—and waits until the mother bird leaves. Then she swoops in, removes one of the host's eggs, and lays her own right in its place. The egg even mimics the color and pattern of the host's eggs! It's a brilliant, if rather sinister, evolutionary adaptation. 

And then, when the cuckoo chick hatches—usually before the host's own chicks—it has this instinct to push the other eggs or hatchlings right out of the nest. So the poor host parents end up working themselves to exhaustion feeding this massive, demanding chick that isn't even theirs, while their own offspring are gone. It's terribly sad, really, but fascinating from a biological standpoint. The ancient Greeks actually wrote about it. Aristotle mentioned it in his *History of Animals*...

Oh, dear me. Cuckoo birds. I’ve done it again, haven't I? I am so terribly sorry, doctor. My mind just latches onto these things. You were asking if the thoughts feel separate from me. Yes, they do. Like an intruder in the nest, I suppose. I really must try to stay focused.
Do you feel like you have to perform these routines in order to reduce or prevent some dreaded event or situation from happening?

Prevent something dreaded? Well, yes, I suppose that's the crux of it, isn't it? What brings me in is that I’ve gotten stuck doing these little routines—washing my hands again after handling my wrist brace, rechecking the stove and the front door, silently counting through steps before I leave the house. I do it because I feel like if I don't, something terrible might happen. 

But it's quite frustrating, because these routines are starting to make me late for things, even when I know perfectly well I’ve already done enough. It reminds me of the timekeeping mechanisms they used to have in the old railway stations. Have you ever seen the inner workings of a Victorian station clock? They were absolute marvels of engineering. 

The mechanism was driven by a heavy weight, usually suspended on a cable, and regulated by a pendulum. But the really fascinating part was the escapement—the part that actually ticks. The most common type was the deadbeat escapement, invented by George Graham in the early 18th century. It was called "deadbeat" because the second hand didn't recoil; it just ticked forward and stopped dead. It made the clocks incredibly accurate, which was essential for the railways, of course. 

Before the railways, every town just kept its own local time based on the sun. Bristol time was about ten minutes behind London time, for instance. But once the trains started running, they needed a standardized time so the timetables would work and trains wouldn't collide. So the Great Western Railway introduced "Railway Time" in 1840, which eventually became Greenwich Mean Time. The station clocks were the masters, and the guards carried these beautiful pocket watches that they had to synchronize with the station clock before every journey...

Oh, good heavens. Victorian clocks now. I am so sorry, doctor. I've done it again. You were asking if I do these routines to prevent something dreaded? Yes, exactly. I get stuck washing, checking the stove and door, and counting steps, just to stave off some vague disaster, and it's making me constantly late. I do apologize. I don't know why my mind insists on taking these little detours today.

Does it prevent something bad? The mechanism was driven by a heavy weight, usually suspended on a cable, and regulated by a pendulum. But the really fascinating part was the escapement—the part that actually ticks. The most common type was the deadbeat escapement, invented by George Graham in the early 18th century. It was called "deadbeat" because the second hand didn't recoil; it just ticked forward and stopped dead. It made the clocks incredibly accurate, which was essential for the railways, of course. 

Before the railways, every town just kept its own local time based on the sun. Bristol time was about ten minutes behind London time, for instance. But once the trains started running, they needed a standardized time so the timetables would work and trains wouldn't collide. So the Great Western Railway introduced "Railway Time" in 1840, which eventually became Greenwich Mean Time. The station clocks were the masters, and the guards carried these beautiful pocket watches that they had to synchronize with the station clock before every journey...

Oh, good heavens. Victorian clocks now. I am so sorry, doctor. I've done it again. You were asking if I do these routines to prevent something dreaded? Yes, exactly. I get stuck washing, checking the stove and door, and counting steps, just to stave off some vague disaster, and it's making me constantly late. I do apologize. I don't know why my mind insists on taking these little detours today.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of recurrent, intrusive thoughts (ugly little thoughts) and compulsions to perform specific rituals (washing hands, checking the stove and door, silently counting steps) in order to reduce or prevent some dreaded event, are characteristic of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD). The patient's difficulty in stopping these thoughts and the significant distress they cause, further support this diagnosis.
